Let \(a=d_5\) and \(b=d_6\). Then \(a<b\), and

\[
n=a^2+b^2.
\]

Since \(a,b\mid n\), we get

\[
a\mid b^2,\qquad b\mid a^2.
\]

Also, there are exactly \(4\) divisors less than \(a\), so every proper divisor of \(a\) is among them; hence \(\tau(a)\le 5\). Similarly, \(\tau(b)\le 6\).

Checking the possible forms from these divisor-count constraints, the only viable case is

\[
a=pq,\qquad b=p^2q
\]

with distinct primes \(p<q\). Now \(b\) has exactly \(6\) divisors, so the five divisors below \(b\) must be precisely the proper divisors of \(b\). Thus \(a=pq\) is the largest proper divisor of \(b=p^2q\), giving \(p<q\).

Now

\[
n=(pq)^2+(p^2q)^2=p^2q^2(p^2+1).
\]

The factor \(p^2+1\) is a divisor of \(n\) below \(b=p^2q\), so it must equal one of the proper divisors of \(b\). Since \(\gcd(p^2+1,p)=1\), it cannot be \(1,p,p^2\), and it is less than \(pq\); hence

\[
p^2+1=q.
\]

For this to be prime, \(p\) must be even, so \(p=2\), giving \(q=5\). Therefore

\[
a=10,\qquad b=20,\qquad n=10^2+20^2=500.
\]

Indeed, the divisors of \(500\) begin

\[
1,2,4,5,10,20,\ldots
\]

so \(d_5=10\), \(d_6=20\), and \(10^2+20^2=500\).

\[
\boxed{500}
\]
